newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco asks to delay Fla secondhand smoke lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco asks to delay Fla secondhand smoke lawsuit.

text.p: The tobacco industry Tuesday asked a Florida judge to delay the trial of a landmark secondhand smoke class action lawsuit filed by airline flight attendants, saying there were dozens of witnesses still to be deposed.
Trial of the lawsuit, known as Broin v. Philip Morris Cos Inc. et al, was scheduled to begin June 2, a date set eight months ago.
Dade County Circuit Judge Robert Kaye did not rule on the motion for a postponement, but was expected to decide within a few days.

Attorney Hugh Whiting, representing R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, said there were at least 50 depositions of expert witness to be done in the next 20 days, in addition to about 30 lay witnesses.

He also suggested the court still needed to hear arguments on whether the lawsuit should be decertified as a class action because of difficult legal issues surrounding the trial of a case with 60,000 plaintiffs.
"We need at least an additional 30 days to have a fair chance at a fair trial," Whiting said.
The lawsuit claims damages on behalf of flight attendants who allegedly contracted lung diseases and other ailments on the job from secondhand smoke on U.S. passenger jets.

Plaintiffs' attorneys, who in the past have accused the tobacco industry of delaying tactics, argued against any delay, noting that the lawsuit had been filed six years ago and saying that thousands of flight attendants had made plans to be in Miami for the June 2 start.
"It's not going to be a perfect trial, but it's going to be a fair trial," attorney Stanley Rosenblatt said.

Rosenblatt said that the industry wanted the delay to allow more time for ongoing "secret negotiations" between state attorneys general and the tobacco industry aimed at settling smoking-related litigation.
"We don't want to have our day in court snatched away by some politically ambitious attorneys general," he said.
During a three-hour hearing Tuesday, Kaye denied a motion made by the tobacco companies to strike some of the diseases the plaintiffs claim were caused by secondhand smoke.
The lawsuit names about two dozen ailments, including lung and various other types of cancer, cardiovascular and heart diseases and other illnesses.

Whiting argued that the "named" plaintiffs in the case -- those representing some 60,000 flight attendants who are members of the class -- are alleged to have just six of the two dozen diseases cited in the lawsuit and as a result, the remainder should be stricken.
"We don't have clarity as to what is to be tried," Whiting said.
But Kaye, in denying the request, said if the plaintiffs were able to prove that secondhand smoke caused all the diseases, it did not matter whether "named" plaintiffs had the ailments.
"We're going with the original number of diseases and class representatives. If they can't prove it, they can't prove it," he said.

In a trial plan ruling last week, Kaye decided that "common issues" regarding the cause of diseases and the tobacco industry's liability would be heard in the trial's first stage with individual claims in the second stage.
The two sides have argued numerous bones of contention in the final days leading up to trial, including the issue of what the lawyers are allowed to say in public.

In a ruling signed Friday, Kaye turned down a tobacco industry demand for a "gag order" to "muzzle" Rosenblatt. The industry claimed Rosenblatt had tried to prejudice potential jurors by releasing to the media transcripts of depositions of tobacco executives.
Kaye repeated a warning to the lawyers to be "circumspect in any public statement" and said failure to comply could bring about a contempt of court citation or a gag order.
